_about: Hand-maintained overviews of W3C work closely related to WCAG. Reviewed weekly (see claude/wcag3-weekly-runs.md). scripts/check-related-standards.mjs refreshes the ACT rule counts and reports when a tracked /TR/ document has a new publication date; it does not rewrite the narrative. Every fact here must cite an entry in that group's sources. Avoid quotation marks in text fields: check-quotes.mjs verifies every quotation of four words or more.

groups.name: ARIA
groups.fullName: Accessible Rich Internet Applications Working Group
groups.tagline: The roles, states and properties that tell assistive technology what a custom control is and what it is doing.

stats.label: Companion specs also in draft (all updated Sep to Oct 2026)

overview: WAI-ARIA is a W3C standard, not a guideline. It defines attributes such as role, aria-expanded and aria-describedby that let a page describe custom widgets to assistive technology. The ARIA Working Group also writes the mapping specs (Core-AAM, HTML-AAM, Accname) that tell browsers how to pass HTML and ARIA through to each operating system's accessibility API.

WCAG does not require ARIA, but much of WCAG 2.2 success criterion 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value is met in practice through it, and the ARIA techniques in Understanding WCAG are sufficient techniques for several criteria. When ARIA changes what a role means or how a name is calculated, the way those criteria are tested changes with it.

current.title: WAI-ARIA 1.2
current.note: The version to build and test against today.

current.title: ARIA in HTML
current.note: Which ARIA roles and attributes are allowed on which HTML elements. The rules most linters check.

current.title: Accessible Name and Description Computation 1.1
current.note: How an element's accessible name is worked out.

current.title: Core Accessibility API Mappings 1.1
current.note: How ARIA maps to platform accessibility APIs.

current.title: Digital Publishing WAI-ARIA Module 1.1 and DPub-AAM 1.1
current.note: Roles for books and long-form publishing.

current.title: WAI-ARIA Graphics Module 1.0 and Graphics-AAM 1.0
current.note: Roles for charts and structured graphics.

current.title: ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)
current.note: Patterns and examples. Not a standard, and it has its own task force.

inDevelopment.title: WAI-ARIA 1.3
inDevelopment.summary: First public draft January 2024. The editor's draft was updated 2 October 2026. At the ACT Task Force on 25 June 2026 this was described as the last review before Candidate Recommendation.
changes: New roles: mark, suggestion and comment (for highlighted, inserted, deleted and annotated content), and sectionheader and sectionfooter (a header or footer for one section rather than the whole site).
role=image added as a synonym for role=img.
New properties: aria-description (a description as a string, not an ID reference), aria-braillelabel and aria-brailleroledescription (braille-only labels).
aria-details can point to more than one element, and aria-errormessage becomes an ID reference list.
ariaNotify, a script API for asking assistive technology to announce something without a live region.
aria-hidden=true is no longer allowed on the document root, and aria-hidden=false now means the same as leaving it off.
An accessible name is no longer required on alertdialog, dialog, form, grid and radiogroup. A combobox may now open a menu, and aria-expanded is removed from listbox.

inDevelopment.title: Core Accessibility API Mappings 1.2
inDevelopment.summary: Platform mappings for the 1.3 roles and properties.

inDevelopment.title: Accessible Name and Description Computation 1.2
inDevelopment.summary: The next naming algorithm. The ACT Task Force deferred reviewing its changes until wide review.

inDevelopment.title: HTML Accessibility API Mappings 1.0
inDevelopment.summary: How each HTML element is exposed to accessibility APIs.

inDevelopment.title: SVG Accessibility API Mappings
inDevelopment.summary: Joint work with the SVG Working Group. The draft warns that it is early, contains outdated information, and should not be implemented from.

connection.wcag22: No change to WCAG 2.2 itself. ARIA 1.3 changes what correct markup looks like, so it changes how 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value and 1.3.1 Info and Relationships are tested: for example, a dialog without a name stops being an ARIA authoring error, though WCAG may still expect one.
connection.wcag3: The WCAG 3 draft has provisions written around the same ideas, and in early October 2026 a set of upstream PRs (#883 to #897) was moving several of them onto the defined term programmatically determinable. These are the provisions to read alongside ARIA:

future.what: The current charter targeted ARIA 1.3 completion in Q3 2026. As of October 2026 it is still a Working Draft, so that date has slipped.
WAI lists an updated ARIA 1.3 draft for September to November 2026, ahead of Candidate Recommendation.
The current charter ends. A draft charter runs 1 January 2027 to 31 December 2028.

The draft charter makes ARIA a Living Recommendation: new features chosen in March 2027, a call for review of amendments in March 2028, and an amended Recommendation in December 2028. It names no ARIA 1.4 or 2.0. The ACT Task Force heard in June 2026 that ARIA will become evergreen, with numbering possibly revisited later.

New deliverables in the draft charter: AT-Driver (a standard way for test tools to drive screen readers), CSS Accessibility API Mappings, and PDF Accessibility API Mappings. MathML-AAM is listed as tentative.
Expect version numbers to matter less. Teams will need to track which features browsers and screen readers support rather than which ARIA version they target.

doNow.action: Keep building and testing against ARIA 1.2 and ARIA in HTML.
doNow.why: Both are Recommendations, and they are what browsers, linters and audit tools implement today.
ARIA in HTML lists where a role is redundant or not allowed. Fewer ARIA attributes means less to retest as 1.3 lands.

hedge.action: Try aria-description and the new roles only where support is confirmed.
hedge.why: They are in a draft. Check current browser and screen reader support before relying on them for a WCAG pass.

hedge.action: Review any aria-hidden on html or body.
hedge.why: 1.3 disallows aria-hidden=true on the document root. It was always a bad idea, and soon it will be an authoring error too.

wait.action: Do not swap live regions for ariaNotify yet.
wait.why: It is a new script API in a draft spec. Live regions keep working, so build a fallback first.
At the ACT Task Force in June 2026, only one screen reader was reported to support the braille attributes.

watch: The 2027 to 2028 charter being approved, and which features are picked in March 2027
Accname 1.2 changes that alter how accessible names are calculated
ACT rules updated for ARIA 1.3 (ACT issue 2400)

sources.title: WAI-ARIA 1.3 editor's draft and change log

groups.name: WCAG2Mobile
groups.fullName: Guidance on Applying WCAG 2.2 to Mobile Applications
groups.group: Mobile Accessibility Task Force (AG Working Group)
groups.tagline: How each WCAG 2.2 success criterion reads when the thing being tested is a native or hybrid app screen instead of a web page.
overview: There is no separate W3C accessibility standard for mobile apps, and WCAG2Mobile will not be one. It is an informative Group Note that explains how the existing WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA criteria apply to native apps, mobile web apps and hybrid apps on phones and tablets. It says itself that it does not set requirements.

It matters because laws increasingly apply WCAG to apps. The US Department of Justice ADA Title II rule applies WCAG 2.1 Level AA to state and local government apps. WCAG was written for pages, so terms like web page, set of web pages and user agent need interpreting. WCAG2Mobile is the W3C's attempt to write those interpretations down.

current.title: WCAG 2.2
current.note: First published October 2023; this is the December 2024 update. Applies to app content as written. Several 2.1 and 2.2 criteria were added with touch screens in mind, such as 1.3.4 Orientation, 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures and 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum).

current.title: WCAG2ICT
current.note: Guidance on Applying WCAG 2 to Non-Web ICT. Covers software in general, including apps, for WCAG 2.0 to 2.2 at A and AA. WCAG2Mobile is modelled on it.

current.title: Mobile Accessibility mapping (2015)
current.note: How WCAG 2.0 applied to mobile. Its last editor's draft was in December 2018.

inDevelopment.title: WCAG2Mobile
inDevelopment.summary: First draft published 6 May 2025 by the Mobile Accessibility Task Force, which regrouped in January 2024. A second draft, covering criteria with small and medium differences from the web reading, was presented to the AG Working Group on 15 September 2026.
changes: Web page becomes screen or view, and the unit of conformance is a single screen.
Set of web pages becomes set of screens, rather than WCAG2ICT's set of software.
Content, user agent and closed functionality are each given mobile readings.
Examples of mobile notes: a long press is not a keyboard shortcut under 2.1.4, and 1.4.12 Text Spacing does not apply when the platform offers no way to override text style.

Still marked work in progress in the published draft: 1.3.1, 1.3.3, 1.3.5, 1.4.3, 1.4.4, 1.4.10, 1.4.11, 1.4.13, 2.1.1 and 2.1.2, among others. The criteria with the largest differences are left for a later draft.

connection.wcag22: No change to the standard. WCAG2Mobile changes how an auditor reads a criterion for an app, not what the criterion says. In the AG discussion on 15 September 2026 it was noted that the DOJ web rule references WCAG2ICT but not WCAG2Mobile, which is not finished.
connection.wcag3: The Mobile Accessibility Task Force said on 15 September 2026 that it would review the WCAG 3 draft published on 10 September and send feedback. An open upstream proposal (PR #880, not merged) would say WCAG 3.0 focuses on web content and is not considered complete for software. Mobile-relevant provisions in the current draft include:

future.what: WAI lists an updated WCAG2Mobile draft for this window.
Task Force session at TPAC 2026 in Dublin covering mobile, ACT and techniques.
Guidance for the criteria with the largest deviations from the web reading, plus guidance at the principle and guideline level.
Publication as a final Group Note, as WCAG2ICT was. It stays informative. After that the Task Force may turn to mobile techniques.

Whether the scope widens. At the 15 September meeting one participant asked the group to consider a broader scope, and several others argued the narrow version fills a real gap for developers and auditors.

doNow.action: Audit apps against WCAG 2.2 A and AA using WCAG2ICT's software readings.
doNow.why: That is the finished W3C guidance today, and it is the one the DOJ rule points to.
Screen as the unit of conformance, and set of screens, are the interpretations most likely to change how you scope an audit.

hedge.action: Note where your audit relies on a WCAG2Mobile reading.
hedge.why: It is a draft. Recording which calls depend on it makes them easy to revisit when the next draft lands.

wait.action: Do not cite WCAG2Mobile as a requirement in contracts or reports.
wait.why: The draft itself says it is inappropriate to cite it as anything other than work in progress.

watch: The next published draft and which criteria leave work-in-progress status
The large-deviation criteria, especially 1.4.4 Resize Text, 1.4.10 Reflow and 2.1.1 Keyboard
Any legal reference to WCAG2Mobile once it is final

groups.name: COGA
groups.fullName: Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force
groups.group: COGA Task Force (joint AG and APA Working Groups)
groups.tagline: Research and design guidance for people with cognitive and learning disabilities, including needs WCAG's testable criteria do not reach.
overview: COGA is a task force shared by the Accessibility Guidelines and Accessible Platform Architectures Working Groups. It does not write a standard. It writes research and design guidance, and it reviews WCAG drafts from the point of view of people with cognitive and learning disabilities.

Its main document, Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities, describes itself as supplemental guidance beyond WCAG 2.2. Following it is not needed for conformance. Its importance for WCAG 3 is that many cognitive needs are hard to write as pass or fail tests, and COGA is pushing for them to be covered by WCAG 3 assertions instead.

current.title: Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities
current.note: Eight objectives, with user stories, design patterns, personas and usability testing guidance.

current.title: WCAG 2.2 criteria that address cognitive needs
current.note: For example 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), all new in 2.2. Date shown is the December 2024 update of WCAG 2.2.

inDevelopment.title: Cognitive Accessibility Research Modules
inDevelopment.summary: Five first drafts published together on 5 February 2026. Each covers user needs, barriers, possible directions and open research questions.
changes: Cognitive Accessibility Research Modules (the overview).
Voice Systems and Conversational Interfaces.
Technology Assisted Indoor Navigation and Wayfinding.
Online Safety and Wellbeing (Algorithms and Data).
Supported Decision-Making Online.

inDevelopment.title: Next three research modules
inDevelopment.summary: On 14 September 2026 the task force set three modules as its 2026 priority, plus a new cover paper introducing all the modules.
changes: Trigger warnings.
User testing.
AI and safety.

inDevelopment.title: WCAG 3 review
inDevelopment.summary: A provision-by-provision review of the WCAG 3 draft, aiming to finish by the end of 2026. Feedback on user needs for each guideline may run into early 2027.

connection.wcag22: No change. Making Content Usable sits beside WCAG 2.2 as advice, and it is the best single source for cognitive issues a 2.2 audit will not catch.
connection.wcag3: WCAG 3 has far more cognitive coverage than 2.2, much of it as assertions: statements that an organisation did something, such as usability testing, rather than a pass or fail test. In the 14 September minutes a COGA member stressed that assertions matter for concerns that cannot be written as testable requirements. Draft provisions close to COGA's work include:

future.what: The three new research modules reach final edit and pre-publication. Getting one module ready takes about a month.
Finish the WCAG 3 provision review, if possible.
Update the Supported Decision-Making module.
A new version of Making Content Usable. On 14 September the task force agreed to wait because of the WCAG 3 review and research module load.
How many COGA needs end up as WCAG 3 assertions, and whether assertions count toward conformance or only toward higher reporting tiers. That depends on the conformance model, which is not settled.

doNow.action: Use Making Content Usable as a design checklist.
doNow.why: It is finished, it is free, and its patterns work no matter how WCAG 3 lands.

doNow.action: Run usability tests that include people with cognitive disabilities.
doNow.why: Several WCAG 3 assertions describe exactly this kind of testing, and it finds problems automated tools cannot.

hedge.action: Read the research module that matches your product.
hedge.why: Voice, wayfinding, safety and decision-making each preview needs WCAG 3 may later address.

wait.action: Do not treat research modules as requirements.
wait.why: They are first drafts that describe open questions, not rules.

watch: Publication of the trigger warnings, user testing and AI and safety modules
COGA feedback filed on WCAG 3 provisions
The new AG task force on assertions
Any restart of Making Content Usable

groups.name: ACT
groups.group: ACT Task Force (AG Working Group) and ACT Rules Community Group
groups.tagline: A shared format for writing accessibility test rules, so two tools testing the same criterion reach the same answer.
overview: ACT exists because tools disagree. The ACT Rules Format is a W3C Recommendation that says how a test rule must be written: what it applies to, what it expects, its assumptions and worked pass and fail examples. Rules written in that format are then checked against real tools.

Two groups share the work. The ACT Rules Community Group writes rules, which have no formal W3C standing. The ACT Task Force in the AG Working Group maintains the format and reviews rules for approval, which needs at least one tool or methodology to implement the rule fully. Approved rules are still informative and are not required to determine WCAG conformance.

current.title: ACT Rules Format 1.1
current.note: The current format. It coexists with 1.0 and is not fully backward compatible.

current.title: ACT Rules on the WAI site
current.note: {act.total} rules listed: {act.approved} approved, {act.proposed} proposed and {act.deprecated} deprecated. {act.noCriterion} map to no WCAG success criterion (mostly ARIA checks).

inDevelopment.title: What changed in ACT Rules Format 1.1
inDevelopment.summary: Candidate Recommendation 19 August 2025, Recommendation 5 February 2026 with no changes in between.
changes: Accessibility requirements are now marked as conformance requirements or secondary requirements.
Applicability may now be subjective, and the objective and plain-language rules were relaxed from must to should.
Accessibility Support and Assumptions move under a Background section, with optional Related Rules and Other Resources.
Each rule must say which format version it targets, and Change Log is renamed Rule Versions.
A new Implementations section says how to judge whether a tool's check is consistent with a rule.
Outcomes can now be cantTell and untested as well as passed, failed and inapplicable.

inDevelopment.title: Rules in progress
inDevelopment.summary: Recent Task Force work includes a glossary review, a new resizing rule, and an impact review of ARIA 1.3 on existing rules (ACT issue 2400), which found the impact small.

connection.wcag22: ACT rules map to WCAG 2 success criteria and to ARIA. When a tool says it implements an ACT rule, you can read the rule to see exactly what it tests and, just as usefully, what it assumes and leaves out.
connection.wcag3: The rules list maps only to WCAG 2 and ARIA today. There are no ACT rules for WCAG 3 provisions yet, which fits a draft where nothing has reached refining status. ACT is on the agenda for the TPAC 2026 session on 29 October. The 1.1 changes for subjective applicability and the cantTell outcome are the kind WCAG 3's less binary provisions would need, though no group has said so.

future.what: Proposed rules move to approved as tools implement them. Counts on this page refresh weekly from the WAI rules data.
ACT is on the agenda for the TPAC 2026 session in Dublin.
Rules updated for ARIA 1.3 changes such as names no longer required on dialog, and possible push-back on the braille attributes.
When ACT rules start being written for WCAG 3. That likely waits until WCAG 3 provisions stabilise.

doNow.action: Ask your testing tool vendor which ACT rules it implements.
doNow.why: The implementation reports show which rules each tool fully or partly matches, which tells you where its results can be trusted.

doNow.action: Use ACT rule examples to settle disputes.
doNow.why: Each rule has passed and failed examples. They are a neutral reference when a tool and a tester disagree.

hedge.action: Treat proposed rules as signals, not verdicts.
hedge.why: They are community rules without formal standing until approved.

wait.action: Do not build WCAG 3 test suites yet.
wait.why: There are no ACT rules for WCAG 3, and the provisions are still changing.

watch: Any ACT rules or test work for WCAG 3 provisions
TPAC 2026 outcomes on ACT and techniques
